small_guidance:
- Add larger tile configs targeting M=1024, N=8192, K=8192: try `BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=4` and `BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=256, BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=4` — N is large so favor wider N tiles to maximize L2 reuse of the X rows.
- Pre-transpose `W` once in `__init__` (store as `[K, N]` contiguous) so the inner `tl.load` on B is contiguous along N (BLOCK_N inner) instead of strided along K — this typically gives 10-20% on K-heavy GEMMs. Cache the transposed weight as a buffer to avoid per-forward transpose cost.
- Bump `num_stages` to 5 for the largest BLOCK_K configs to better overlap K-loop loads, and add a `GROUP_M=16` variant since M/BLOCK_M is small (8-16 row tiles) and larger groups improve L2 reuse across N tiles.
large_guidance:
- Switch the kernel layout to load weight as `[K, N]` (transpose once at init, store as a registered buffer). Then both A and B have their contiguous axis on the inner load dimension, enabling vectorized 128-bit loads and removing strided B accesses; this is the single largest structural win available.
- Consider a split-K or stream-K design: with K=8192 and only 8 row tiles (M=1024 / BLOCK_M=128), the grid is small (~256 programs) and underutilizes the 128 SMs of the 4090 when BLOCK_N is large. A persistent / stream-K kernel that splits the K reduction across more programs and atomically accumulates (or uses a two-stage reduction) would raise occupancy.
- Use TF32 `tl.dot(..., allow_tf32=True)` (default) and ensure inputs stay fp32; alternatively, cast inputs to bf16 inside the kernel for the matmul (output kept fp32 in the accumulator) since the 5e-2 tolerance easily permits it — this roughly doubles tensor-core throughput on Ada.
